canonical_topic: AC vs. DC transmission (Edison vs. Westinghouse)
definition: The historical competition between Edison's direct current (DC) system and Westinghouse's alternating current (AC) system, resolved in favor of AC because it allowed voltage to be transformed up or down.
core_idea: Edison's DC system suffered from voltage drop over distance with no efficient way to step voltage up or down, which meant generators had to be small and located near end-users; Westinghouse's AC system (based on Tesla's design) used transformers to repeatedly step voltage up or down, letting a single large plant serve a wide area and multiple customer voltage needs, which is why AC became the universal transmission standard.
key_points: DC transmission loses voltage over distance with no efficient step up/down mechanism
DC's limitation implied small, local generation near end-users
AC, using transformers, can step voltage up or down multiple times along the transmission path
AC let one large plant serve a wide area and serve both high-voltage industrial and low-voltage residential customers
The greater efficiency of large generation plants tipped the outcome toward AC becoming the universal standard
